It has been an important medium through which values, traditions, relationships, responsibilities and collective memory have been transmitted across generations. Karnataka Explores New Education Model Diwali 2026: School Holidays – Check State-Wise Holiday Schedule Cyclone Murasu: Schools Closed In Andhra Pradesh’s NTR District Today Amid Heavy Rain Alert Today, this formative role is facing a new challenge. The digital ecosystem is increasingly competing with the family in shaping individual aspirations, perceptions, relationships and behaviour. The concern is not simply that children are spending excessive time on smartphones. It extends to changing expectations of marriage, parenthood, personal freedom, relationships and responsibility towards the elderly. The central question is whether the Indian family can adapt to the digital age without surrendering its role in shaping individual judgement and social values. The Family: An Institution of Cognitive Formation The traditional Indian family provided an informal system of education, socialisation, emotional support and behavioural regulation. Children learnt not only through instructions but also by observing how elders behaved, disagreements were resolved and responsibilities were shared. Freedom existed alongside obligations, and individual achievements were understood within a larger framework of family relationships. The traditional family was not without shortcomings. It could be hierarchical, restrictive and unequal, particularly towards women and younger members. As greater independence, educational opportunities, financial autonomy and freedom of choice are legitimate aspirations the objective, therefore, should not be to preserve every traditional practice but to retain the formative and supportive functions of the family while allowing its structure to evolve. The Indian family was already changing through urbanisation, migration, employment opportunities and smaller households. Research using National Family Health Survey data has documented a decline in average household size and a gradual reduction in multigenerational households (Lekhwani, n.d.; Mondal & Pradhan, 2025). These changes are not necessarily undesirable, but they redistribute responsibilities for childcare, eldercare and emotional support. The digital revolution has arrived while families are still adjusting to these transitions.
